name: Composite
intent: Treat single objects and groups of objects through the same interface, so trees can be handled uniformly.
scenario: A file explorer has files and folders. Folders hold files and other folders. The total size of anything, file or folder, is one call.
problem: Folders contain files and other folders, to any depth. Client code that asks for a total size has to check whether each item is a file or a folder and recurse by hand, everywhere it is needed.
solution: Give files and folders one shared interface with getSize(). A file returns its own size. A folder returns the sum of calling getSize() on its children, which may themselves be folders. The client just calls getSize() on whatever it holds.
pain: Client code checks the type of every item
Recursion over folders is repeated in each feature
Adding a new kind of item means touching every type check
Client must know the tree's structure
benefits: One call, getSize(), works on a file or a whole tree
New item types (shortcut, archive) just implement the interface
Client treats leaves and groups the same
whenToUse: Your data forms a tree: menus, file systems, UI components, org charts
Clients should treat single items and groups uniformly
Operations naturally recurse over the structure
whenNotToUse: The structure is flat: a plain list is enough
Leaves and groups have very different operations, so a shared interface becomes awkward
You need strong type safety on which nodes can have children
pitfalls: Interface bloat: leaves inherit add() and remove() they cannot use
Cycles: a folder containing itself makes getSize() loop forever
Deep trees can overflow the stack on recursion
Hard to restrict what a composite may contain

roles.label: Component
roles.description: Common interface for leaves and composites.

roles.label: Leaf
roles.description: An item with no children that does the real work.

roles.label: Composite
roles.description: Holds children (any Component) and delegates to them.

quiz.question: A file explorer uses Composite: File and Folder both implement Item.getSize(). The team adds a new Archive item (a zip file that reports its unpacked size). What must change?
options: Add an Archive class that implements Item, leaving client code and Folder as they are
Add a branch for Archive in Folder.getSize(), since folders do the summing for their children
Update every feature that totals sizes, so each of them checks for Archive explicitly
Make Archive a subclass of Folder, so it is summed with the other folders
quiz.explanation: A new item type only needs to implement the shared interface, because Folder and the client call getSize() on whatever they hold. Branching on Archive reintroduces the type checks that Composite removes.

quiz.question: A user drags folder A into its own subfolder B. Later, a size query on A throws a stack overflow. What is the right fix?
options: Catch the stack overflow in getSize() and return the size computed up to that point
Cap the tree depth at 50 and ignore deeper children when summing, so recursion stops
Cache each folder's size, so repeat calls return before the loop is reached
Reject a child in add() if it is the parent or one of its ancestors
quiz.explanation: The tree now contains a cycle, so recursion never ends. The fix is to keep it a tree by checking in add(). Catching the error returns a wrong total, a depth cap silently drops data, and a cache does not help the first call.

quiz.question: In a Composite, the Item interface has getSize(), add() and remove(). Developers keep calling add() on File objects, and File.add() throws at runtime. Which change keeps getSize() uniform and removes this class of bug?
options: Make File.add() quietly ignore the call, so that nothing throws any more
Make every file a Folder with an empty child list, so add() always works on any item
Move add() and remove() to Folder, and keep getSize() on Item
Make File.add() turn the file into a folder on the first call and keep the child in it
quiz.explanation: Child management only makes sense for composites, so moving it to Folder gives compile-time safety while shared operations stay on the common interface. Ignoring the call hides mistakes, and turning files into folders blurs what a file is.
